body.v: Perfect, that works for me. I've put the final figures on CloudDrive so we can both edit them. CloudDrive will ask you to sign in with your work email.
On Monday you wrote: "Send me the figures when they're final and I'll check them."

hotspots.explain: It really is Elena's address, and the conversation really happened. A hijacked account passes every address check.
A new shared file, and you have to sign in with your work email to see it. That is exactly the kind of request used to harvest login details.
clouddrive-view.example is not CloudDrive's domain, which is clouddrive.example. Whoever controls Elena's account can send any link they like.
Your own sentences, quoted word for word: it sounds genuine. But anyone reading Elena's inbox can copy them.

who.prompt: Who is really writing to you? Read the address, not just the name.
who.answer: Not necessarily Elena. The address and the conversation are genuine, so her account may have been hijacked. Only a phone call will tell you.
choices: Maybe Elena, maybe someone who hijacked her account
Definitely Elena, since the conversation is genuine

emotion.prompt: Which feeling is this email pressing on?
emotion.answer: Wanting to help, and a little hurry to get the report finished together.
choices: Wanting to help finish the report

ask.prompt: What does it actually want you to do?
ask.answer: Sign in to CloudDrive through a link. Your work login details would go straight to whoever controls Elena's account.
choices: Sign in by going through a link
Reply with your date of birth

verify.prompt: How can you check through a channel you control?
verify.answer: Don't touch the link. Open CloudDrive yourself and look for the file, or call Elena on a number you already know.
choices: Open CloudDrive yourself, or call Elena
Sign in, the conversation is genuine
Reply to ask whether it is really her

actions.label: Open CloudDrive yourself to look for the file, or call Elena
actions.consequence: No file by that name. On the phone, Elena is baffled: she never sent that email.

actions.label: Click the link and sign in
actions.consequence: The page records your work login details and passes them to whoever controls Elena's account.

actions.label: Reply: "Is this really you?"
actions.consequence: Whoever holds the account says yes. You asked the impostor.

actions.label: Tell the IT team that Elena's account may have been hijacked
actions.consequence: The IT team can lock the account before it is used against anyone else.

attacker_reveal: You'd never seen this one before: my link slipped into a real conversation, under a real colleague's name. The questions hadn't changed, though. Who is really writing, and how do you check?
